evidence.quote: [/page/0/Text/8] Thirty-four adolescents (mean age 15.2 years, SD = 1.5) referred by school counsellors were randomly assigned to either cCBT or a computer-administered attention placebo program with psychoeducational content (CPE).

[/page/6/Text/10] 34 were randomized; 17 participants were assigned to each group. In the cCBT group, all but one of the participants (94%) completed the full program and posttreatment [/page/8/Table/2] cCBT (n = 17)

evidence.section_title: A Pilot Double Blind Randomized Placebo Controlled Trial of a Prototype Computer-Based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Program for Adolescents with Symptoms of Depression
evidence.quote: [/page/0/Text/8] The objective of this study was to examine the feasibility, acceptability, and effects of The Journey, a computerized cognitive behavioural therapy (cCBT) program for depressed adolescents.
computerized cognitive behavioural therapy (cCBT)
[/page/2/Text/9] We conducted a double blind randomized placebo controlled trial (RCT) in which a cCBT program was compared with a computerized program with a brief psycho-educational content (CPE).

[/page/2/Text/11] Participants were informed that they would complete one of two computer programs: one with practical strategies that can "teach them ways to deal with depression" or a comparison programme where the emphasis was on "healthy living and having fun which may also decrease depression".
We created two programs – an active program with CBT content (cCBT) and a control attention placebo program based on psycho-educational content (computerized psychoeducation i.e. CPE).
[/page/4/Text/5] Our cCBT program covers well-established core cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) techniques.
[/page/4/Text/7] The CPE program served as an attention placebo control and was void of any CBT content.
[/page/8/Table/2] Notes: cCBT – computerized cognitive behavioural therapy
[/page/8/Text/8] 10 by participants from cCBT group
cCBT – computerized cognitive behavioural therapy

[/page/11/Text/10] At the end of treatment 88.2% of those who had received cCBT had a response rate (30% or greater reduction in CDRS-R score) compared with 47.1% of those on CPE (Fisher's exact text p=.025).

[/page/12/Text/5] In the cCBT group, 22.2% guessed correctly, 11.1% guessed incorrectly and 66.7% did not know; in the CPE group, none guessed correctly, 41.7% guessed incorrectly and 58.3% did not know.
[/page/12/Text/7] We successfully piloted a purpose-developed adolescent-specific computer-based CBT program

[/page/2/Text/7] Participants were invited to the study if they had a raw score of 30 or more on Depression Rating Scale Revised (CDRS-R) (Poznanski and Mokros, 1996) or if they scored 76 or above on Reynolds' Adolescent Depression Scale-2nd Edition (RADS-2) (Reynolds, 2002). A score of 30 or more on CDRS suggests that it is "possible that a depressive disorder might be confirmed in a comprehensive diagnostic interview" (Poznanski and Mokros, 1996) and similarly, a cut of 76 on RADS-2 is suggestive of the risk for major depressive symptoms (Reynolds, 2002).

Participants were students aged 13 to 18 years who had referred themselves for help with low mood to school counsellors in eight urban high schools in Auckland over a period of one school year.

[/page/2/Text/11] School counsellors screened adolescents to determine the eligibility for the study. Participants were informed that they would complete one of two computer programs: one with practical strategies that can "teach them ways to deal with depression" or a comparison programme where the emphasis was on "healthy living and having fun which may also decrease depression".
